questionText: How do you find and fix N+1 queries in EF Core?
shortAnswer: One query per parent plus one per child (logs show the pattern). Fix with eager loading (Include/ThenInclude), projection (Select with children), or explicit batch loads — then verify a constant query count regardless of parent count.
detailedAnswer: Shape: foreach (var o in orders) { o.Lines.Count } with lazy loading (or lazy-ish manual queries) = 1 + N round trips. Detection: EF logs (repeated identical SELECTs with varying ids), MiniProfiler/EF events, or tests asserting query counts. Fixes: (1) Include(o => o.Lines).ThenInclude(l => l.Product) — single query with JOINs (cartesian blowup on multiple collections — see split queries); (2) Projection: Select(o => new Dto { Lines = o.Lines.Select(...) }) — one query, tight columns, no tracking (preferred for reads); (3) Explicit batch: load all lines for all ids in one Where(l => ids.Contains(l.OrderId)) then ToLookup join in memory (two queries total, full control). Split queries (AsSplitQuery): one query per Include path (avoids cartesian explosion; more round trips but smaller payloads — measure). Lazy loading proxies: convenient, N+1-prone, serialization-cycle-prone — disable by default (use LazyLoadingEnabled false + explicit loads). Verification: integration test asserting SQL count == constant for N parents (query-count assertions are the only durable defense).
internalWorking: Lazy loading emits a query per navigation access (proxy override or ILazyLoader callback). Include generates LEFT JOINs (cartesian product across multiple collections — row explosion); split queries issue sequential SELECTs per path (no duplication, more trips). Projections generate correlated subqueries/joins in one statement.
realWorldUsage: Master-detail endpoints, report hydration, feed enrichment, and any loop touching navigations.
commonMistake: Lazy loading in loops (the classic), Include-everything (cartesian explosion on 2+ collections — split or project), and fixing N+1 with caching (masks it — fix the queries).
technicalConversation: Ask how many queries their detail endpoint emits — logs don't lie; 1+N versus constant is the reviewable number.
interviewFollowUp: When is a split query slower than a single join query despite avoiding duplication?
keyTakeaway: N+1 = per-child queries in a loop. Include, project, or batch — then assert constant query counts.

questionText: How do compiled queries (EF.CompileQuery) speed up hot paths?
shortAnswer: EF.CompileQuery caches the translated SQL + materializer once, skipping per-call translation (expression walk + plan build). Worth it for high-frequency queries with varying parameters; negligible for cold paths. Measure translation time first.
detailedAnswer: Normal path per execution: build expression tree → translate (expensive: model metadata walks, SQL gen) → execute. Compiled: static readonly Func<DbContext, TParam, TResult> Q = EF.CompileQuery((DbContext ctx, int id) => ctx.Orders.Where(...).First(...)) — translation once (static init), executions reuse the plan with new parameters. Gains: 10–50% on tiny hot queries (translation dominates), near-zero on heavy queries (execution dominates). Rules: static readonly fields (compile once per AppDomain); parameters only (no captured locals — captured values bake as constants, defeating plan caching AND causing cache pollution); async variant EF.CompileAsyncQuery; split-query + compiled compose. Alternatives that often win more: simpler queries (translation cost follows complexity), projection (less materialization), and proper indexes (execution dominates anyway). Diagnostics: translation time via EF events/logging (QueryExecutionPlanned); plan-cache size counters. When NOT: dynamic shapes (compiled needs fixed shape — dynamic filters need expression-built trees, compiled per shape variant), rarely-run queries, and InMemory tests (no translation to skip — test with real provider).
codeExample:
static readonly Func<AppDbContext, int, Task<Order?>> GetOrder =
    EF.CompileAsyncQuery((AppDbContext db, int id) =>
        db.Orders.Include(o => o.Lines).FirstOrDefault(o => o.Id == id));

Order? order = await GetOrder(db, id); // translation reused, parameter bound
internalWorking: Translation output (shaped query expression + materializer delegates) is cached keyed by the expression structure; parameters flow as DbParameters. Compiled queries pin the plan (no per-call model walk). Captured locals become constant nodes (distinct plans per value — cache bloat + recompile each time).
realWorldUsage: Auth lookups per request, hot config reads, high-RPS detail endpoints, and polling loops.
commonMistake: Captured locals (plan cache pollution — parameters only), compiling dynamic shapes (pointless — shape varies), and optimizing translation when execution/indexes dominate (profile first).
technicalConversation: Ask what fraction of their hot query time is translation versus execution — compiled queries only move the first; indexes and projections move the second.
interviewFollowUp: Why do captured locals defeat compiled queries, and what replaces them?
keyTakeaway: Compile hot fixed-shape queries once; parameters, never captured locals. Measure translation share first.

questionText: When should you use AsSplitQuery versus a single query with Includes?
shortAnswer: Single query for one collection (JOINs fine); split for 2+ collections (avoids cartesian explosion). Split costs extra round trips but smaller payloads; single costs duplication. Measure payload vs trips for your shape — projection often beats both.
detailedAnswer: Cartesian math: order × 10 lines × 5 payments = 50 rows per order (order columns repeated 50x) — with 3 collections it explodes multiplicatively. Single query wins when: one collection included, small sets, or latency dominates (one trip). Split (AsSplitQuery) wins when: multiple collections, large sets, or duplication dwarfs trip cost (typical: 2–5x less data, 2–4 trips). Configuration: global UseQuerySplittingBehavior(SplitQuery) vs per-query AsSingleQuery/AsSplitQuery (per-query is explicit — prefer it). Gotchas: split queries aren't atomic by default (concurrent modifications between trips → inconsistent snapshot — wrap in a transaction with RepeatableRead/Snapshot when consistency matters); split + Take/Skip applies per... no — Take applies to the root with split followers (correct paging, more trips); split queries and MARS/provider multi-result requirements (SQL Server fine; some providers restrict). Alternative champion: projection (Select with nested collections — one query, no duplication, no tracking — usually the best read answer). Decision order: project > split > single-with-joins for reads; load-then-attach for writes.
internalWorking: Single: one SQL with JOINs (row count = product). Split: sequential SELECTs (root + one per collection path) correlated by key, assembled client-side. Projection: one SELECT with scalar/collection subqueries (no duplication, minimal columns).
realWorldUsage: Detail endpoints with multiple child lists, export queries, and aggregate dashboards.
commonMistake: Include-everything singles (payload explosion), split without consistency needs (snapshot skew — transaction it), and ignoring projection (the usual winner).
technicalConversation: Ask for the row multiplier on their heaviest detail query — product-of-collections math decides single/split/project in one line.
interviewFollowUp: Why do split queries need transaction wrapping for consistency, and what isolation suffices?
keyTakeaway: One collection → join; many → split; reads → project. Snapshot consistency needs a transaction across trips.

questionText: How do you stream large query results without materializing them (AsAsyncEnumerable)?
shortAnswer: await foreach over the IQueryable/IAsyncEnumerable with cancellation: rows stream from the reader, memory stays flat. Keep the context alive during streaming, avoid buffering operators mid-stream, and never return the stream past the context lifetime.
detailedAnswer: Pattern: await foreach (Order o in db.Orders.Where(...).AsAsyncEnumerable().WithCancellation(ct)) { await ProcessAsync(o); } — DbDataReader streams, EF materializes per row, GC reclaims behind you. Rules: no ToList (that is the materialization you are avoiding); no OrderBy-without-index on huge sets (sort spills server-side — keyset instead); no lazy navigations mid-stream (N+1 per row — project/include first); cancellation wired (WithCancellation — kill long streams on shutdown/timeout); context lifetime spans the loop (no repository-method boundary mid-stream — stream inside the scope). Batching variant: Chunk over the async stream for bulk writes (1000-row transactions). Export variant: write CSV lines as you stream (constant memory for GBs). Monitoring: rows/sec + memory flatline prove streaming (sawtooth = buffering leak). Alternatives: server-side cursors/keyset paging (equivalent, more trips, resumable), raw SqlDataReader for max control (no materializer overhead), and COPY/BULK for DB-to-DB moves (never through app memory).
internalWorking: AsAsyncEnumerable exposes the provider's async enumerator (DbDataReader ReadAsync loop + per-row materialization). No buffering beyond the reader's network buffers. Disposal (await using / end of foreach) closes the reader + returns the connection. Cancellation aborts the command server-side.
realWorldUsage: CSV/PDF exports, migration backfills, search indexing, bulk email rendering, and ETL extracts.
commonMistake: ToList before streaming (defeats it), lazy navs in the loop (N+1 × millions), unindexed OrderBy on streams (server sort spill), and returning the enumerable past context disposal.
technicalConversation: Ask for memory shape during their biggest export — flat (streaming) versus proportional (materialized) is observable in one graph.
interviewFollowUp: Why can't you return an IAsyncEnumerable from a repository method that disposes its DbContext?
keyTakeaway: await foreach + cancellation, no ToList, context spans the loop. Flat memory at any scale.

questionText: How do you build dynamic filters (optional criteria) without branching queries everywhere?
shortAnswer: Compose IQueryable conditionally (if (x != null) query = query.Where(...)) — one final SQL, no duplication. For OR-groups use PredicateBuilder/OrElse expressions; for fully dynamic UIs build expression trees or use a filter DSL (never string-concatenated SQL).
detailedAnswer: AND-filters compose trivially: IQueryable<Order> q = db.Orders; if (from != null) q = q.Where(o => o.Date >= from); if (term != null) q = q.Where(o => o.Customer.Contains(term)); — deferred composition emits one SQL with all applied predicates (the standard search-endpoint pattern). OR-groups need expression combination: PredicateBuilder.Or / manual Expression.OrElse with a parameter-rebinding visitor (LinqKit AsExpandable or hand-rolled) — Func<> delegates can't combine into trees (invoke nodes don't translate — expressions only). Dynamic sort: OrderBy via property-name maps (switch returning Expression<Func<T, object>> per allowed column — allowlist, never raw strings into Dynamic LINQ without validation). Fully dynamic UIs: filter DTO → expression builder per field type (string→Contains, range→comparisons, enum→equality) composed with AndAlso. Paging/sorting applied last, Count for totals (two queries — standard). Testing: combinatorial fixtures (each criterion alone + pairs) asserting SQL shape or result sets; empty-criteria returns everything (document!).
internalWorking: Each Where appends an AND predicate node to the same expression tree (no execution until enumerated). OR needs single-tree combination (OrElse with unified ParameterExpression — hence builders/visitors). Dynamic-LINQ strings parse to trees at runtime (translation as usual, injection-safe via parameterization — still allowlist columns).
realWorldUsage: Search/filter endpoints, admin grids, report builders, and advanced-find UIs.
commonMistake: Branching full queries per combination (2^n explosion), Func predicates in trees (invoke nodes — untranslatable), raw column strings (injection/shape errors — allowlist), and OR via Union of full queries (works but heavier than OrElse).
technicalConversation: Ask how many query shapes their search endpoint can produce versus how many code paths build them — one composable path is the maintainable answer.
interviewFollowUp: Why can't you combine Func<T,bool> delegates into an EF predicate, and what replaces them?
keyTakeaway: AND-filters compose by chaining Where. OR needs expression combination. Allowlist dynamic sorts.

questionText: How does query-plan caching and parameterization affect LINQ performance?
shortAnswer: EF caches translated plans keyed by query shape; constants baked into trees create distinct plans per value (cache pollution + recompile). Capture locals as parameters (the default for variables), avoid string-concatenated values and per-value constants, and watch plan-cache counters.
detailedAnswer: Mechanics: captured variables → DbParameters (one plan, many executions — plan reuse, index-friendly). Inline constants (hardcoded literals, computed values folded into the tree, loop-varying expressions) → distinct plans per value (recompile each time + cache bloat — the 'N plans for N ids' syndrome). Offenders: string interpolation into queries (use parameters!), DateTime.Now inline (evaluates per translation AND pollutes — hoist to local), loop-built predicates with embedded values (parameterize or batch), and .Contains(hugeList) (parameter explosion — thousands of parameters; chunk or join to a temp set instead). SQL Server specifics: parameter sniffing (first execution's plan reused — occasionally wrong for skewed data; OPTION(RECOMPILE)/optimize-for hints via raw SQL or plan guides for the outliers). Diagnostics: plan-cache size + compile counters, EF translation logs, and SQL with @p0 (parameterized, good) versus literals (bad). Compiled queries pin one plan deliberately (hot fixed shapes). Testing: execute same shape with different values, assert single plan (test hooks on the cache or timing deltas).
internalWorking: Translation output cached in the query cache keyed by expression structure (constants part of the key). Parameters map to DbParameters (server plan reuse + sniffing). Contains(list) expands to IN (@p0..@pn) — plan size and server limits (2100 params SQL Server!) bound it.
realWorldUsage: Hot filtered endpoints, polling loops, batch lookups, and reporting queries.
commonMistake: Inline DateTime.Now (recompile + wrong-per-day semantics), mega-Contains (parameter limits + huge plans), and interpolated SQL fragments (injection + plans).
technicalConversation: Ask what their SQL looks like — @p0 parameters (healthy) versus literal storms (cache pollution) is visible in one log sample.
interviewFollowUp: What is parameter sniffing, and when does plan reuse hurt?
keyTakeaway: Variables parameterize (one plan); literals inline (plan per value). Chunk giant Contains; hoist DateTime.Now.

questionText: How do you sort stably at scale (large datasets, distributed shards)?
shortAnswer: Total order requires a unique tiebreak everywhere: OrderBy(key).ThenBy(id) in DB (indexed), merge-sorted streams by key for shards (k-way merge), and cursor/keyset paging for stable walks. Sorting without a unique key is nondeterministic — at any scale.
detailedAnswer: Single DB: index on (sortKey, id) makes ORDER BY + keyset both fast and stable (covering index avoids sorts entirely — 'index provides order'). Sharded/distributed: sort each shard, k-way merge by key (PriorityQueue<(key, shardIdx)> — O(n log shards)), tiebreak by (key, shard, id) for determinism. In-memory large: OrderBy buffers fully (spill to disk? no — OOM; external sort via chunk-sort-merge for >RAM). Time-series: partition by time, sort within partitions (bounded memory). UI: stable sort + keyset cursors (offset drifts under inserts). Ties across shards: global unique ids (snowflake/UUIDv7 carry time-ordering — sortable and unique). Testing: duplicate-key fixtures asserting deterministic order across runs (flaky-order tests catch missing tiebreaks). Monitoring: sort spills/tempdb (SQL warnings), merge fan-in lag per shard, and page-drift complaints ( tiebreak missing).
internalWorking: DB sorts use indexes (ordered scans, no sort operator) or sort operators (memory grant, tempdb spill). K-way merge is O(n log k). Keyset cursors seek via the same index (constant per page). UUIDv7/Snowflake ids sort by creation time (index-friendly inserts, no page splits).
realWorldUsage: Global feeds, multi-shard listings, time-series rollups, merge replication, and distributed search.
commonMistake: Sorting without unique tiebreak (flaky pages), offset across shards (compounding drift), in-memory sort of DB-scale data (OOM — sort at source), and random UUID PKs (index fragmentation + unsortable).
technicalConversation: Ask how their global feed orders across regions — single-sort-key answers hide the tiebreak and merge questions.
interviewFollowUp: Why do time-ordered unique ids (UUIDv7) solve two problems at once for distributed sorting?
keyTakeaway: Unique tiebreak everywhere, index-backed order, k-way merge across shards. No tiebreak, no determinism.

questionText: How do you test LINQ logic reliably (pure pipelines, EF queries, edge data)?
shortAnswer: Test pure operators against fixed in-memory data (exact sequences), EF queries against a real provider (SQLite/Testcontainers — never InMemory for translation), and edges explicitly (empty, nulls, ties, duplicates, case variants, huge counts via chunking assertions).
detailedAnswer: Layers: (1) Pure pipeline tests: static data in, exact expected out (SequenceEqual) — predicates, projections, groupings, custom operators. Table-driven (Theory + MemberData) for edge matrices. (2) Provider tests: same shapes against SQLite file (translates!) or Testcontainers SQL Server/Postgres (exact provider semantics — null handling, collation, functions). InMemory provider: fine for logic scaffolding, worthless for translation (translates nothing — green lies). (3) Property tests (FsCheck/CsCheck): invariants over random inputs (sorted output, count preservation, idempotence). (4) Performance tests: BenchmarkDotNet for hot operators (not unit suites — separate, gated). Fixtures: empty/null/tie/duplicate/case-variant/unicode/large (chunked) datasets as shared builders. Assertions: exact sequences (not counts alone — content proves), SQL shape snapshots (ToQueryString contains JOIN/GROUP BY — guards translation regressions), and query-count assertions (N+1 guards). Flakiness: no DateTime.Now (inject TimeProvider/seeded clocks), no unordered comparisons (sort or set-compare), no shared static data (fresh fixtures).
internalWorking: In-memory LINQ runs delegates (C# semantics); provider tests run translation + SQL (provider semantics — nulls, collation, functions differ). The gap between them is exactly what the two layers cover. FsCheck generates edge inputs systematically (shrinking to minimal failures).
realWorldUsage: Pipeline unit suites, EF integration suites, migration validators, and query-shape regression gates in CI.
commonMistake: InMemory-only EF tests (translation blind), count-only assertions (content unproven), DateTime.Now fixtures (flaky), unordered comparisons (flaky), and shared mutable fixtures (cross-test pollution).
technicalConversation: Ask what their EF tests run against — InMemory-only is the standard false-confidence setup; SQLite/Testcontainers is the fix.
interviewFollowUp: Why does testing against InMemory give false confidence for EF queries specifically?
keyTakeaway: Pure logic in memory (exact), provider behavior on real providers, edges always. InMemory never proves translation.

questionText: How do you handle slowly changing dimensions and late-arriving facts in LINQ pipelines?
shortAnswer: Version dimensions (effective-from/to + current flag); join facts to the version effective at event time (range join), defaulting to current for late data within tolerance. Recompute affected windows on late arrival (idempotent upserts) instead of appending corrections.
detailedAnswer: SCD-2 shape: dimension rows carry (BusinessKey, ValidFrom, ValidTo, IsCurrent). Fact join: facts.SelectMany(_ => dims).Where(f => f.Key == d.Key && f.Time >= d.From && f.Time < d.To) (range join — index on (Key, From, To); large sets prefer SQL temporal tables or interval indexes). Late facts (event time < watermark): route to recompute (re-aggregate affected windows, upsert results — idempotent keys make reruns safe) versus drop-with-log (beyond tolerance — business policy). Current-view queries: .Where(d => d.IsCurrent) (indexed flag) or max-ValidFrom per key (GroupBy + MaxBy). Audit: keep superseded rows (never update history — append versions; corrections are new versions). EF: temporal tables (SQL Server SYSTEM_VERSIONING — FOR SYSTEM_TIME queries) automate this; LINQ-side range joins for provider-agnostic code. Testing: backdated fixtures asserting correct-version joins + late-arrival recomputes (exact expected windows).
internalWorking: Range joins are nested-loop-ish without interval indexes (bound data sizes or push to SQL with temporal support). Version chains (prev-pointer) allow point-in-time walks. Idempotent upserts (MERGE/ON CONFLICT) make recomputes safe.
realWorldUsage: Price histories, org hierarchies over time, compliance snapshots, slowly-changing reference data, and event-time analytics.
commonMistake: Joining to current-only (history rewrites silently), unbounded range joins (cartesian risk — index + bound), and appending corrections instead of recomputing (double-counts).
technicalConversation: Ask what 'the price on March 3rd' means in their system — current-price answers reveal history blindness; versioned answers reveal maturity.
interviewFollowUp: Why are corrections-as-new-versions safer than in-place updates for historical facts?
keyTakeaway: Version dimensions, join as-of event time, recompute idempotently on late data. Never rewrite history.

questionText: How do you keep huge LINQ pipelines debuggable in production (observability without drowning)?
shortAnswer: Instrument stage boundaries (counts + timings via Tap/keywords), log query shapes (not full data), sample payloads, and correlate with operation ids. Debug with materialized stage dumps in dev; monitor with counters/histograms in prod — never full dumps in prod.
detailedAnswer: Dev: stage-bisection with ToList + counts (the standard technique), Tap probes (pass-through logging operator, removed after), ToQueryString for SQL, and LINQPad-style dumps of fixtures. Prod: per-stage counters (in/out counts — drop ratios reveal filter bugs), elapsed histograms per stage (which link is slow), shape logs (query hash + row counts, never PII/payloads), sampled payload logging (1/1000 with PII scrubbing), and correlation ids flowing through the pipeline (trace a single item end-to-end). EF: sensitive-data logging OFF in prod (parameter values are PII — shape + counts only), query tags (.TagWith("pipeline:orders-daily") attributing SQL to code), and slow-query alerts on translation + execution. Alerts: stage-drop anomalies (sudden 100% filter rate = upstream schema change), latency regression per stage, and memory growth on buffering ops. Post-incident: replay from staged snapshots (materialized stage outputs persisted at boundaries enable exact replays — the case for boundary materialization beyond performance).
internalWorking: Tap is a streaming iterator (O(1) memory, logs on completion/disposal — counts log at enumeration end, including early-exit partial counts). Counters/histograms aggregate in process (Meter/Activity APIs) exported to Prometheus/AppInsights. Query tags become SQL comments (traceable in server logs/profilers).
realWorldUsage: ETL observability, report pipeline SLAs, feed-health dashboards, and slow-query attribution.
commonMistake: Full payload logging in prod (PII + volume incidents), no stage boundaries (unlocalizable slowdowns), sensitive-data logging left on (credential leaks into logs), and untagged queries (unattributable slow SQL).
technicalConversation: Ask how they would find which stage of a 12-step pipeline slowed down — per-stage timings (not total) is the only answer that works.
interviewFollowUp: Why are staged snapshots valuable beyond debugging — what incident capability do they enable?
keyTakeaway: Count and time every stage; log shapes not data; tag queries. Boundaries make pipelines observable and replayable.
